title: Airbnb house rules template: copy, adapt, and make them stick
summary: Free Airbnb house rules template with cabin, condo, family and pet-friendly versions, plus how Airbnb's standard rules work and where rules need to appear.
body_markdown:
[All posts](https://prohost.ai/blog)


**House rules are the part of a listing guests agree to and almost never read. They matter on the few nights something goes wrong: the extra guests, the party, the dog nobody mentioned. On those nights, a rule that was written down and agreed to at booking is something you can act on. A rule that lived in your head is not. Below is a house rules template you can copy, variants for cabins, condos, family homes and pet-friendly stays, and where each rule needs to appear so guests actually see it.**


## Key takeaways


- **Four in ten listings have no house rules on file.** Of 13,663 active listings on ProhostAI, 40% have none recorded. If yours is one of them, the template below takes ten minutes.
- **Start with Airbnb's standard rules.** Maximum guests, pets, smoking, quiet hours, events and commercial photography are built in. Set them first, then add your own.
- **Write rules as facts about the home, not warnings to the guest.** "The hot tub closes at 10 p.m. for the neighbors" explains itself. "NO HOT TUB AFTER 10!!!" reads like a threat.
- **Fewer rules get followed better.** Keep the additional rules to what you'd actually act on. Everything else is guidebook material.
- **Repeat the important ones where guests look.** The listing, the check-in message and the guidebook. One mention at booking is not enough.

## How Airbnb's house rules work


Airbnb splits house rules into two kinds (per Airbnb's[house rules help article](https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/472) and its hosting guide on[setting helpful house rules](https://www.airbnb.com/resources/hosting-homes/a/setting-and-creating-helpful-house-rules-21) , both checked 19 November 2026):


- **Standard house rules.** You pick from a fixed set: maximum overnight guests, pets, smoking, quiet hours, events, commercial photography, and lock up at checkout. In Airbnb's words, "in most cases, the standard house rules will cover the core expectations you need to convey to your guests."
- **Additional rules.** Anything else, written in your own words, such as shoes off indoors or no daytime visitors. Airbnb flags additional rules that may not comply with its policies when you save them, and says they "should be reasonable" for the type of listing and local law.


Three details from those pages are worth knowing before you write:


1. **Changes only apply to future reservations.** A rule you add today doesn't bind the guest who booked last month. Tell current guests by message if it matters.
2. **Guests are expected to follow your house rules** under Airbnb's ground rules for guests, and Airbnb says a host can cancel without fees or other consequences if a guest breaks a house rule during the stay.
3. **Fines don't belong in your rules.** Airbnb says hosts generally shouldn't impose fines or penalties. If an HOA or local government fines for something, note that in the local rules section of your listing instead.


## The house rules template


Copy this, delete what doesn't apply, and replace the brackets. Set the standard rules in Airbnb's settings first; the lines marked *(standard)* should match those settings exactly.


> **Welcome to \[listing name\].** A few rules keep the home in good shape and the neighbors happy. Thank you for following them.
>
>
> **Guests** *(standard)* : Up to \[number\] guests stay overnight. Day visitors are welcome until \[time\], up to \[number\] people. Please let us know before inviting anyone.
>
>
> **Quiet hours** *(standard)* : \[10 p.m.\] to \[8 a.m.\]. We're in a residential neighborhood and sound carries from the \[deck / pool / yard\].
>
>
> **Events and parties** *(standard)* : Not allowed. Small dinners with your own group are fine.
>
>
> **Smoking and vaping** *(standard)* : Not allowed inside or on the \[deck / balcony\]. \[Outdoor area, if any\] is fine. Please use the ashtray provided.
>
>
> **Pets** *(standard)* : \[Not allowed / Allowed with approval; see pet rules below\].
>
>
> **Parking** : \[Number\] cars in \[the driveway / spaces numbered X\]. Please don't park on the street or block the neighbors' driveways.
>
>
> **Shoes** : \[Please take shoes off at the door / no rule\].
>
>
> **Trash and recycling** : Bins are \[location\]. Pickup is \[day\]; if you're here the night before, please roll them to the curb.
>
>
> **Outdoor areas** : The \[pool / hot tub / fire pit\] is open \[hours\]. Children must be supervised by an adult at all times.
>
>
> **Security cameras** : There is a camera covering \[the driveway / the front door\]. There are no cameras inside the home.
>
>
> **Checkout** *(standard: lock up)* : By \[time\]. Start the dishwasher, leave used towels in the bathtub, take your trash to the bins, and lock the door behind you.
>
>
> **If something breaks** : Please tell us. Accidents happen, and we'd rather fix it before the next guest arrives.


Two lines do more work than they look. The day-visitor line closes the gap between "four guests" and "four guests plus eight friends for dinner". The "if something breaks" line turns a damage conversation into a maintenance one.


On cameras: Airbnb has its own rules on disclosing cameras and devices, separate from house rules. Check them in Airbnb's help center for your listing before you write the line, and keep the house rule consistent with what you've disclosed.


## Variants by property type


### Cabin with a hot tub or fire pit


> **Hot tub** : Open until \[10 p.m.\]. Shower before using it. No glass in or around the tub. Children under \[age\] need an adult in the tub with them. Please replace the cover after every use so it stays warm and safe.
>
>
> **Fire pit and fireplace** : Use only the firewood provided. Never leave a fire unattended, and put it out fully with water before bed. If there's a burn ban in \[county\], the fire pit is closed; we'll message you if one is in effect.
>
>
> **Wildlife** : Keep trash in the \[bear-proof bin / garage\] and don't leave food on the deck overnight.
>
>
> **Driveway** : \[The last stretch is steep and gravel. In snow or ice, use the lower parking area / 4WD recommended.\]


### Condo or building with an HOA


> **Building rules** : The \[association / building\] has its own rules, and fines for breaking them are passed to the owner. Please follow them; the main ones are below.
>
>
> **Pool and gym** : Open \[hours\]. Bring the wristband or fob from the \[drawer by the door\]. Guests under \[age\] need an adult.
>
>
> **Parking** : Space \[number\] only. Visitor parking is \[location\] and limited to \[hours\].
>
>
> **Noise** : Quiet hours are \[10 p.m.\] to \[8 a.m.\] in the whole building, including balconies.
>
>
> **Elevator and moving** : Please don't prop doors or use the service elevator without booking it.
>
>
> **Trash** : The chute is \[location\]. Recycling goes to \[location\].


### Family home


> **Children** : We provide \[a crib, a high chair, outlet covers\]. The \[stairs / pool\] are not gated, so please supervise young children.
>
>
> **Personal items** : The \[closet / room\] marked private is off-limits.


### Pet-friendly stay


> **Pets** : Up to \[number\] \[dogs / pets\] under \[weight\], with approval before arrival. Please tell us the breed and size when you book.
>
>
> **Inside** : Pets stay off the beds and sofas. Please bring their own bedding; we provide \[bowls, a towel by the door\].
>
>
> **Alone in the home** : Pets can't be left alone \[at all / for more than X hours\], and should be crated if left.
>
>
> **Outside** : Please pick up after your pet in the yard and on walks. Bags are \[location\].
>
>
> **Pet fee** : \[amount\] per stay, which covers the extra cleaning.


A pet fee is a fee you charge through Airbnb's pricing settings, not a fine. Keep it in the listing price, not just in the rules.


## What's enforceable and what's a wish


Every rule should pass one test: if a guest broke it, would you act on it? If yes, it's a rule. If no, it's a preference, and it belongs in the guidebook.


Rule Usually enforceable Why


Maximum guests Yes A standard rule, and over-occupancy is a safety and insurance issue


Events and parties Yes A standard rule, and the one neighbors and cities care about most


Quiet hours Yes A standard rule; easier to enforce with a noise sensor than with a complaint


Smoking indoors Yes A standard rule; leaves evidence


Pets without approval Yes A standard rule


Shoes off indoors Rarely An additional rule you won't act on; keep it friendly


Load the dishwasher No A checkout request, not a rule. Keep the checkout list short


Fines for breaking rules No Airbnb says hosts generally shouldn't impose them


"Usually enforceable" means the rule is clear, agreed to at booking, and something you'd act on. What happens next depends on the situation and Airbnb's process, not on how firmly you worded it.


## Where the rules need to appear


A rule a guest saw once, three weeks before arrival, is a rule they've forgotten. Put the important ones in three places:


1. **The listing.** Airbnb's standard rules and your additional rules. This is the version guests agree to.
2. **The check-in message.** One line with the two or three rules that matter most for that home, usually quiet hours, guest count and parking. The[check-in instructions guide](https://prohost.ai/blog/airbnb-check-in-instructions) shows where that line goes.
3. **The guidebook.** The full list, with the reasons. Guests who want details look here, and it's the version you can update for current guests too.


Keep the wording identical in all three. A guest who sees "quiet after 10" in one place and "quiet after 11" in another will pick the later one.


For the rest of the stay's messages, the[message templates hub](https://prohost.ai/blog/airbnb-message-templates) covers the welcome, checkout and review request.

## Keep it running


House rules go stale. A new hot tub or a new parking ordinance, and the rules no longer match the home.


**Grace, the Guidebook Manager AI employee,** audits each listing's guidebook for missing or stale sections, including house rules, and suggests updates when recurring guest questions show a gap. Any guidebook change from her own runs needs a person's approval before it publishes.


**Answers come from the same rules.** When a guest asks "can we have friends over for dinner?", AI replies in ProhostAI draw on your listing details, guidebook and what it has learned about the property, so the answer matches your rules instead of contradicting them.


**Quiet hours can watch themselves.** With a noise sensor connected through[smart devices](https://prohost.ai/features/smart-devices) , you set a quiet-hours window, and a reading over your threshold in that window can send the current guest an automatic message.


What still needs a person: the judgment call. Whether a noise alert means a party or a loud movie, whether a guest broke the guest-count rule or had friends over for an hour, and whether to cancel. Those decisions are yours.

## FAQ


**What should Airbnb house rules include?** At minimum: maximum guests, quiet hours, events, smoking, pets and checkout. Those are Airbnb's standard rules. Add parking, outdoor areas, trash and anything specific to your home that you'd actually act on.


**How many house rules is too many?** If the additional rules don't fit on one phone screen, there are too many. Move preferences, like how to use the coffee machine, into the guidebook.


**Can I charge guests for breaking house rules?** Airbnb says hosts generally shouldn't impose fines or penalties. A pet fee or extra guest fee set in your pricing is different; that's a price, not a fine.


**Do new house rules apply to guests who already booked?** No. Airbnb applies changes only to future reservations. If a change matters for a current guest, message them.


**What's the best way to enforce quiet hours?** A noise sensor and a friendly automatic message when it goes over your threshold. It reaches the guest while the noise is still happening.


## The takeaway


Set Airbnb's standard rules first, then add only the additional rules you'd act on. Write them as facts about the home, keep the wording the same in the listing, the check-in message and the guidebook, and let a sensor or an AI watch the rules you can't see being broken.
